title: Infinite Loop Bug #1
description: A JavaScript function to count down from 10 runs forever and freezes the browser tab.
hint: Look carefully inside the while loop — what should change with each iteration so the condition eventually becomes false?

title: Off-By-One Error #2
description: A function that should return the last element of an array always throws an 'undefined' error instead.
hint: Arrays are zero-indexed — if an array has 3 items, what is the index of the last one?

title: Wrong Comparison Operator #3
description: A login check always grants access even when the password is wrong.
hint: There is a difference between = and === in JavaScript — one assigns, one compares.

title: Scope Bug in Loop #4
description: A loop creates 5 buttons, but clicking any of them always shows '5' instead of the button's number.
hint: The var keyword has function scope not block scope — by the time any button is clicked, what value does i have?

title: Missing Return Statement #5
description: A function that doubles a number always returns undefined when the result is used elsewhere.
hint: The calculation happens inside the function — but how does the value get back to the caller?

title: Python Indentation Error #6
description: A Python function to check if a number is even or odd gives a syntax error and won't run at all.
hint: Python uses indentation to define code blocks — every line inside a function must be indented consistently.

title: Recursive Stack Overflow #7
description: A Python recursive function to calculate factorial causes a RecursionError for any input.
hint: Recursion needs to move toward the base case with each call — what should change between each recursive call?

title: Dictionary Key Error #8
description: A Python script counts word frequencies but crashes with a KeyError on the first new word it encounters.
hint: You can't increment a value that doesn't exist yet — you need to handle the case when a word appears for the first time.

title: Promise Chain Error #9
description: An API call chain silently swallows errors — failed requests are never reported to the user.
hint: Promise chains need error handling — what method catches rejected promises?

title: Type Coercion Bug #10
description: A function that adds two numbers from form inputs always concatenates them as strings instead of adding.
hint: HTML input values are always strings — JavaScript's + operator concatenates strings before it adds numbers.

title: Null Pointer Crash #11
description: A JavaScript function crashes with 'Cannot read properties of null' when trying to update a DOM element that doesn't exist yet.
hint: Always check that querySelector/getElementById returned an element before accessing its properties.

title: Wrong Array Method #12
description: A function meant to transform each item in an array returns undefined because it uses forEach instead of map.
hint: forEach executes a function for side effects but doesn't return a new array. Which array method returns a transformed array?

title: Python Range Stop Exclusive #13
description: A Python loop that should print numbers 1 through 10 stops at 9 because the range stop is exclusive.
code:
for i in range(1, 10): # ❌ stops at 9, not 10
    print(i)
hint: Python's range(start, stop) excludes the stop value — the last number printed is stop - 1.
solution:
for i in range(1, 11): # ✅ range up to 11 to include 10
    print(i)

title: Missing Break in Switch #14
description: A switch statement falls through and executes multiple cases because break statements are missing.
hint: Without a break, switch falls through to the next case. Each case should end with break or return.

title: Async/Await Missing Await #15
description: An async function returns a Promise object instead of the resolved value because await is missing.
hint: In an async function, you must use await before every Promise to get the resolved value.

title: Python Integer Division #16
description: A Python 3 percentage calculator returns 0 for values under 100 because integer division is used accidentally.
hint: // is integer (floor) division in Python. Use / for float division.

title: Event Propagation Bug #17
description: Clicking a card's 'Delete' button also triggers the card's click handler, causing unintended navigation.
hint: Click events bubble up the DOM tree. Stop the event from reaching parent elements.

title: Comparison With NaN #18
description: A validation function never catches invalid numbers because it compares with NaN, and NaN is not equal to anything — including itself.
hint: NaN is never equal to anything, including NaN. Use isNaN() or Number.isNaN() to check for NaN.

title: Python Mutable Class Variable #19
description: All instances of a Python class share the same list because it's defined as a class variable instead of an instance variable.
code:
class ShoppingCart:
    items = []  # ❌ class variable — shared by ALL instances!

    def add_item(self, item):
        self.items.append(item)

cart1 = ShoppingCart()
cart2 = ShoppingCart()
cart1.add_item('Apple')
print(cart2.items)  # ['Apple'] — unexpected!
hint: Class variables are shared across all instances. Move the list initialization into __init__ to make it per-instance.

title: Strict Mode Assignment Error #20
description: A JavaScript module crashes in strict mode because it tries to assign a value to an undeclared variable.
hint: In strict mode, all variables must be declared with let, const, or var before assignment.

title: Array Filter Returns Empty #21
description: An array filter function returns an empty array even though matching elements exist, because the condition is inverted.
hint: The ! operator negates the condition — removing it will filter for users where active is true.
solution:
const activeUsers = users.filter(u => u.active); // ✅ no negation
console.log(activeUsers); // [Alice, Carol] ✅

title: Python List Comprehension Logic #22
description: A list comprehension that should collect even squares returns squares of even numbers only, not even results from all numbers.
code:
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

# Goal: get squares of all numbers that are even when squared
# Bug: filters by input being even, not output being even
even_squares = [n**2 for n in numbers if n % 2 == 0]
print(even_squares)  # [4, 16, 36] — only squares of 2,4,6
hint: Move the condition to check the result (n**2 % 2 == 0) instead of the input (n % 2 == 0).
solution:
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

# If goal is: squares of all numbers, filtered to keep only even squares:
even_squares = [n**2 for n in numbers if (n**2) % 2 == 0]
print(even_squares)  # [4, 16, 36] — all squares of even numbers are even

# If goal is: all squares, keep only even results (same output here but different intent)
all_squares_even = [n**2 for n in numbers if n**2 % 2 == 0]

title: Undefined vs Null Check #23
description: A guard clause fails to catch null values because it only checks for undefined, not null.
hint: Both null and undefined represent 'no value'. Check for both, or use a loose equality check.

title: String IndexOf Misuse #24
description: A function checking if a string contains a keyword gives wrong results when the keyword is at position 0.
hint: indexOf returns 0 when the match is at the start — and 0 is falsy in JavaScript. Compare with -1 instead.

title: Python Walrus Operator Confusion #25
description: A Python while loop reads lines from a file but misses the last line because the condition is checked before assignment.
code:
def read_lines(filename):
    lines = []
    with open(filename) as f:
        line = f.readline()
        while line:  # ❌ reads first line but checks before appending
            lines.append(line)
            line = f.readline()
    return lines  # works but duplicates effort
hint: Use the walrus operator := to assign and check in the while condition simultaneously.
solution:
def read_lines(filename):
    lines = []
    with open(filename) as f:
        while line := f.readline():  # ✅ assign and check in one step
            lines.append(line.strip())
    return lines

title: Prototype Method Override Bug #26
description: A class method accidentally shadows a built-in Array method, breaking all array operations in that scope.
hint: Shadowing native method names causes confusion. Use descriptive domain-specific names instead.

title: Broken Ternary Nesting #27
description: A nested ternary operator returns the wrong value because of incorrect operator precedence without parentheses.
hint: Deeply nested ternaries are hard to read and debug. Use if/else or an object lookup instead.

title: Python f-string Format Error #28
description: A Python f-string crashes with a SyntaxError because curly braces in a math expression conflict with f-string delimiters.
code:
name = 'Alice'
score = 95

# ❌ SyntaxError: mismatched braces
print(f'Player {name} scored {{score}} points')
hint: Double curly braces {{ and }} are escape sequences in f-strings that produce literal { and }. Use single braces for expressions.
solution:
name = 'Alice'
score = 95

# ✅ single braces for variable, double braces for literal { }
print(f'Player {name} scored {score} points')  # Player Alice scored 95 points

# If you want literal curly braces in the output:
print(f'Set: {{1, 2, 3}} and name={name}')  # Set: {1, 2, 3} and name=Alice

title: Incorrect Object Key Access #29
description: A function trying to access a dynamic property of an object always returns undefined because it uses dot notation with a variable name.
hint: To access an object property dynamically using a variable, use bracket notation obj[variable].

title: Missing Default Parameter #30
description: A function crashes when called without the second argument because no default value is provided.
hint: Define a default value for optional parameters using = in the function signature.

title: String Immutability Bug #31
description: A function trying to replace a character in a string by index fails silently because strings are immutable in JavaScript.
hint: JavaScript strings are immutable. Build a new string using slice, split/join, or substring.

title: Python Tuple Immutability #32
description: A function tries to update a coordinate in a tuple and crashes because tuples are immutable in Python.
code:
def move_right(point, distance):
    point[0] += distance  # ❌ TypeError: tuple does not support item assignment
    return point

position = (10, 20)
move_right(position, 5)
hint: Tuples are immutable in Python — create a new tuple instead of modifying the existing one.
solution:
def move_right(point, distance):
    return (point[0] + distance, point[1])  # ✅ return new tuple

position = (10, 20)
new_position = move_right(position, 5)
print(new_position)  # (15, 20) ✅

title: parseInt Radix Missing #33
description: parseInt converts a hex string to decimal but gives the wrong result because the radix parameter is omitted.
hint: Always pass the radix (base) as the second argument to parseInt to avoid ambiguous parsing.

title: Destructuring with Rename #34
description: A destructured variable name conflicts with an existing variable and throws a SyntaxError.
hint: Use destructuring rename syntax { originalKey: newName } to avoid naming conflicts.

title: Python Indeterminate Operator Order #35
description: A Python calculation gives the wrong result because of unexpected operator precedence without parentheses.
code:
def calculate_discount(price, discount_pct):
    # ❌ This calculates price - (discount_pct / 100)
    # not (price * discount_pct) / 100
    final = price - discount_pct / 100
    return final

print(calculate_discount(100, 20))  # 99.8 — wrong! should be 80
hint: Use parentheses to make operator precedence explicit and avoid ambiguity.
solution:
def calculate_discount(price, discount_pct):
    discount_amount = (price * discount_pct) / 100  # ✅ explicit precedence
    return price - discount_amount

print(calculate_discount(100, 20))  # 80.0 ✅

title: Accessing .length on Object #36
description: A function returns undefined when checking the length of an object because objects don't have a .length property.
hint: Objects don't have .length. Use Object.keys(), Object.values(), or Object.entries() to count properties.

title: Python Global vs Local Variable #37
description: A Python function trying to modify a global counter variable creates a new local variable instead, leaving the global unchanged.
code:
counter = 0

def increment():
    counter += 1  # ❌ UnboundLocalError — Python treats as local

increment()
print(counter)  # unchanged
hint: To modify a global variable inside a function, use the 'global' keyword.
solution:
counter = 0

def increment():
    global counter  # ✅ declare intent to modify global
    counter += 1

increment()
print(counter)  # 1 ✅

# Better design: return the new value instead of using globals
def increment_pure(c):
    return c + 1

counter = increment_pure(counter)

title: typeof Checks for Class Instances #38
description: A type guard using typeof incorrectly classifies a class instance as an 'object' instead of identifying it as a specific class.
hint: typeof returns 'object' for class instances. Use instanceof to check the specific class.

title: Array.sort Mutates Original #39
description: A function that should return a sorted copy of an array accidentally mutates the original array.
hint: Array.sort() sorts in place and returns the same array. Copy the array first with [...arr] or arr.slice().

title: Python Exception Too Broad #40
description: A bare except clause catches all exceptions including system exit and keyboard interrupt, making it impossible to stop the program.
hint: Always catch specific exceptions. Bare except or except Exception swallows critical system signals.

title: JSON.stringify Circular Reference #41
description: JSON.stringify throws a TypeError when trying to serialize an object that contains a circular reference.
hint: Break the circular reference or use a replacer function to handle circular structures.

title: Python Set Membership Check #42
description: A function checking if an item is in a large list uses the 'in' operator on a list, giving O(n) lookup instead of O(1).
hint: Convert the list to a set for O(1) average-case membership testing.

title: Incorrect Short-Circuit Evaluation #43
description: A default value assignment using || incorrectly treats 0 and empty string as falsy, replacing valid values with the default.
hint: Use the nullish coalescing operator ?? instead of || when 0 or empty string are valid values.

title: Python Zip Truncation #44
description: A function pairing two lists silently drops elements from the longer list because zip() stops at the shorter one.
code:
names  = ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Carol', 'Dave']
scores = [95, 87, 91]

pairings = list(zip(names, scores))  # ❌ Dave is silently dropped!
print(pairings)  # [('Alice',95), ('Bob',87), ('Carol',91)]
hint: Use itertools.zip_longest to keep all elements from both lists, filling missing values with a default.
solution:
from itertools import zip_longest

names  = ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Carol', 'Dave']
scores = [95, 87, 91]

pairings = list(zip_longest(names, scores, fillvalue=None))
print(pairings)  # [('Alice',95), ('Bob',87), ('Carol',91), ('Dave', None)] ✅

title: Incorrect Spread Merge #45
description: Merging two objects with spread places the defaults last, so they overwrite user values instead of the other way around.
hint: In object spread, later properties overwrite earlier ones. Put defaults first and user preferences last.

title: Python Class Method vs Static Method #46
description: A utility method on a class fails when called on the class itself because it's defined as a regular method requiring self.
code:
class MathUtils:
    def square(self, n):  # ❌ requires instance to call
        return n ** 2

# MathUtils.square(5) crashes — needs self!
# MathUtils().square(5) works but is wasteful
hint: Use @staticmethod for utility methods that don't need access to the class or instance.

title: Missing Array Bounds Check #47
description: A function accessing an array index crashes when the array is empty or the index is out of range.
hint: Always check that an array has elements before accessing by index.

title: Boolean Implicit Conversion #48
description: A function checking for truthy values incorrectly treats the string 'false' as truthy.
hint: URL parameters are always strings. Convert to boolean explicitly by comparing to the string 'true'.

title: Python __str__ vs __repr__ #49
description: A Python class's string representation shows unhelpful memory addresses in the REPL because __repr__ is not defined.
code:
class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

p = Point(3, 4)
print(p)    # <__main__.Point object at 0x7f...> ❌
print([p])  # [<__main__.Point object at 0x7f...>] ❌
hint: Define __repr__ for developer-friendly representation and __str__ for end-user display.

title: setInterval Not Cleared #50
description: A React component that sets up a polling interval causes increasing memory usage and duplicate requests because the interval is never cleared.
hint: Return a cleanup function from useEffect that calls clearInterval to stop the timer when the component unmounts.

title: Python List Slicing Confusion #51
description: A function that should reverse a string uses incorrect slice notation and returns an empty string.
hint: For reverse slicing, omit start and stop: s[::-1] reverses the entire string.

title: parseInt on Float String #52
description: A rounding function uses parseInt on a decimal string and gets unexpected results for values like '9.9'.
hint: parseInt truncates decimal parts. Use Math.round(), Math.floor(), or Math.ceil() for proper rounding.

title: Forgotten await in Loop #53
description: A loop that should process items sequentially runs all promises in parallel because await is outside the loop.
hint: forEach doesn't await async callbacks. Use for...of loop to properly await each iteration.

title: Python Enumerate Start #54
description: A display function shows list items numbered from 0 instead of 1 because enumerate starts at 0 by default.
code:
def display_menu(items):
    for i, item in enumerate(items):  # ❌ starts at 0
        print(f'{i}. {item}')

display_menu(['Coffee', 'Tea', 'Juice'])
# 0. Coffee
# 1. Tea
# 2. Juice  — users expect 1-indexed!
hint: Pass a second argument to enumerate() to specify the starting index.
solution:
def display_menu(items):
    for i, item in enumerate(items, start=1):  # ✅ start at 1
        print(f'{i}. {item}')

display_menu(['Coffee', 'Tea', 'Juice'])
# 1. Coffee
# 2. Tea
# 3. Juice ✅

title: Implicit Return in Arrow Function #55
description: An arrow function trying to implicitly return an object literal returns undefined because the curly braces are parsed as a function body.
code:
const toUser = (name, age) => { name, age }; // ❌ parsed as function body, not object

console.log(toUser('Alice', 30)); // undefined
hint: To implicitly return an object literal from an arrow function, wrap it in parentheses.
solution:
const toUser = (name, age) => ({ name, age }); // ✅ parens force object literal

console.log(toUser('Alice', 30)); // { name: 'Alice', age: 30 } ✅

title: Python sorted() vs list.sort() #56
description: A function returns None because it uses list.sort() which sorts in-place and returns None, instead of returning the sorted list.
code:
def get_top_3(scores):
    return scores.sort(reverse=True)[:3]  # ❌ sort() returns None!

result = get_top_3([50, 90, 70, 80, 60])
print(result)  # None
hint: list.sort() sorts in place and returns None. Use sorted() which returns a new sorted list.
solution:
def get_top_3(scores):
    return sorted(scores, reverse=True)[:3]  # ✅ sorted() returns new list

result = get_top_3([50, 90, 70, 80, 60])
print(result)  # [90, 80, 70] ✅

title: DOM querySelector Typo #57
description: A querySelector call silently returns null because a CSS class selector is missing its dot prefix.
hint: CSS class selectors need a dot prefix. Element selectors have no prefix, and ID selectors use #.

title: Python None Comparison #58
description: A Python function compares a value to None using == instead of 'is', which can give wrong results for objects that override __eq__.
code:
def is_empty(value):
    if value == None:  # ❌ == can be overridden by __eq__
        return True
    return len(value) == 0
hint: Always use 'is None' to check for None — it checks identity, not equality, and can't be overridden.
solution:
def is_empty(value):
    if value is None:  # ✅ identity check — always correct for None
        return True
    return len(value) == 0

# PEP8 enforces: use 'is None' / 'is not None' for None checks

title: Regex Match vs Test #59
description: A regex validation function returns an object (truthy) for every input including invalid ones, because match() is used where test() should be.
hint: Use regex.test(string) to get a boolean, or string.match(regex) to get match details.

title: Python String join Order #60
description: A function joining a list of words into a sentence places the separator on the wrong side, producing garbled output.
code:
words = ['Hello', 'World', 'Python']

# ❌ join is called on the LIST not the separator
sentence = words.join(' ')
print(sentence)  # AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'join'
hint: In Python, join is a string method called on the separator, taking the list as its argument.
solution:
words = ['Hello', 'World', 'Python']

sentence = ' '.join(words)  # ✅ separator.join(iterable)
print(sentence)  # 'Hello World Python' ✅

title: Mutating Props in React #61
description: A child component directly mutates a prop object, causing unexpected behavior in the parent without any React re-render.
hint: Never mutate props directly. Use a callback prop to notify the parent to update its state.

title: Python Deep Recursion Limit #62
description: A recursive tree traversal crashes with RecursionError on deep trees because Python's default recursion limit is 1000.
hint: Convert deep recursion to an iterative approach using an explicit stack.

title: Incorrect CSS Specificity Reset #63
description: Using !important to override styles creates a specificity arms race that makes the CSS unmaintainable.
hint: Refactor to flat, BEM-style selectors with low specificity instead of using !important.

title: Python Generator Exhaustion #64
description: A generator is iterated twice but returns no elements on the second pass because generators are exhausted after one iteration.
hint: Generators can only be iterated once. Store results in a list or recreate the generator for each use.
solution:
def get_evens(n):
    for i in range(n):
        if i % 2 == 0:
            yield i

# ✅ Option 1: convert to list to reuse
evens_list = list(get_evens(10))
print(evens_list)  # [0,2,4,6,8]
print(evens_list)  # [0,2,4,6,8] — list is reusable

# ✅ Option 2: recreate generator each time
print(list(get_evens(10)))
print(list(get_evens(10)))

title: Map with parseInt Radix Issue #65
description: Using parseInt directly as a map callback gives wrong results because map passes index as the second argument, which parseInt interprets as a radix.
hint: map passes (element, index, array) to the callback. parseInt's second argument is the radix — wrap it in an arrow function.

title: Python Dict update() Side Effect #66
description: A function to merge two dicts modifies the original instead of returning a new merged dict.
hint: Create a copy of the base dictionary before updating to avoid mutating the original.

title: Event Delegation Wrong Target #67
description: An event delegated to a parent element targets the wrong element when the user clicks on a child inside the intended target.
hint: Use closest() to find the intended ancestor element even when a child element is clicked.

title: Python frozenset for Dict Keys #68
description: A function using a list as a dictionary key fails with TypeError because lists are unhashable in Python.
hint: Dictionary keys must be hashable. Convert the list to a tuple, which is hashable.

title: Optional Chaining Misuse #69
description: Optional chaining silently returns undefined for a required nested property, hiding a data model error instead of surfacing it.
hint: Use optional chaining only for truly optional properties. Required data should throw explicitly if missing.

title: Python max() on Empty Sequence #70
description: A function finds the maximum score but crashes with ValueError when passed an empty list.
hint: Pass a default value to max() or check for an empty sequence before calling max().

title: Binding Event Listener Creates New Function #71
description: An event listener added with .bind() can never be removed because .bind() creates a new function reference each time.
hint: Store the bound function reference so the same reference can be used for both add and remove.

title: Python Multiline String Indentation #72
description: A Python multiline string inside an indented function includes unwanted leading whitespace in each line.
code:
def get_html():
    return """
        <html>
            <body>Hello</body>
        </html>
    """  # ❌ includes leading spaces due to indentation
hint: Use textwrap.dedent() to remove common leading whitespace from multiline strings.
solution:
import textwrap

def get_html():
    return textwrap.dedent("""
        <html>
            <body>Hello</body>
        </html>
    """).strip()  # ✅ removes indentation

# Or use a raw string without indentation:
def get_html():
    return (
'<html>\n'
'    <body>Hello</body>\n'
'</html>'
    )

title: Forgotten Error Status Check #73
description: A fetch call doesn't handle HTTP error responses like 404 or 500, treating them as successful responses.
hint: Always check res.ok or res.status after fetch — HTTP errors don't cause the promise to reject.

title: Python Complex Number Mistake #74
description: A student writes a Python complex number literal incorrectly, using * instead of j notation.
code:
# ❌ Trying to create 3 + 4i
z = 3 + 4*i  # NameError: name 'i' is not defined

# Or mistakenly:
z = complex(3, 4)  # works but verbose
print(z.real, z.imag)
hint: Python uses 'j' (not 'i') as the imaginary unit suffix in complex number literals.
solution:
z = 3 + 4j  # ✅ Python uses 'j' for imaginary unit
print(z)         # (3+4j)
print(z.real)    # 3.0
print(z.imag)    # 4.0
print(abs(z))    # 5.0 — magnitude

title: Incorrect use of .reduce() #75
description: A reduce function that calculates the total price of cart items returns NaN because the initial value is missing.
hint: Always provide an initial value as the second argument to reduce to ensure the accumulator starts correctly.
solution:
const total = cart.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price, 0); // ✅ start at 0
console.log(total); // 6.5 ✅

title: Python Comparison Chaining Mistake #76
description: A Python developer compares a value against multiple options using 'or' incorrectly, always getting True.
code:
def is_weekend(day):
    return day == 'Saturday' or 'Sunday'  # ❌ always True!
    # Parsed as: (day == 'Saturday') or ('Sunday')
    # 'Sunday' is truthy — always returns 'Sunday'!

print(is_weekend('Monday'))  # 'Sunday' — wrong!
hint: Each comparison must be written explicitly. 'x == a or b' is not the same as 'x == a or x == b'.

title: Template String Backtick vs Quote #77
description: A template literal fails to interpolate variables because it uses single quotes instead of backticks.
hint: Template literals must use backticks (`) not single or double quotes to enable interpolation.

title: Python Counter Most Common #78
description: A function finding the most frequent element crashes on an empty list because most_common() is not called correctly.
code:
from collections import Counter

def most_frequent(items):
    counts = Counter(items)
    return counts.most_common[0][0]  # ❌ missing () — accessing attribute not calling method

most_frequent(['a', 'b', 'a', 'c', 'a'])
hint: most_common is a method — it needs parentheses to be called: most_common(1) or most_common()[0].
solution:
from collections import Counter

def most_frequent(items):
    if not items:
        return None
    counts = Counter(items)
    return counts.most_common(1)[0][0]  # ✅ call with (), then index

print(most_frequent(['a', 'b', 'a', 'c', 'a']))  # 'a' ✅

title: CSS Overflow Hidden Cuts Shadow #79
description: A card's drop shadow is being clipped by its parent container using overflow: hidden.
hint: overflow: hidden clips anything outside the container bounds, including box-shadow. Add padding to the container instead.

title: Conditional State Update in useEffect #80
description: A useEffect updates state inside a condition but the dependency array doesn't include the condition variable, causing stale behavior.
hint: Any value used inside useEffect should be in its dependency array to keep the effect up to date.

title: Python List vs Tuple Return #81
description: A function meant to return multiple values returns a tuple but the caller tries to unpack it as a list, causing index errors.
code:
def get_bounds(numbers):
    return [min(numbers), max(numbers)]  # returns list

min_val, max_val = get_bounds([3, 1, 4, 1, 5])  # works, but...
min_val, max_val, avg = get_bounds([3, 1, 4])  # ❌ ValueError: not enough values
hint: Make sure the number of values returned matches what the caller expects when using tuple unpacking.
solution:
def get_stats(numbers):
    return min(numbers), max(numbers), sum(numbers) / len(numbers)  # ✅ 3 values

min_val, max_val, avg = get_stats([3, 1, 4, 1, 5])
print(f'Min: {min_val}, Max: {max_val}, Avg: {avg:.2f}')

title: Infinity and NaN in Math #82
description: A function calculating average returns Infinity when dividing by zero instead of a sensible fallback.
hint: Always guard against division by zero with an explicit check.

title: Python Strip vs Split #83
description: A CSV parser crashes because it uses strip() where split() should be used, leaving data as one unsplit string.
code:
def parse_csv_line(line):
    return line.strip(',')  # ❌ strip removes chars from edges, not splits

result = parse_csv_line('Alice,30,Engineer')
print(result)  # 'Alice,30,Engineer' — unchanged!
hint: strip() removes leading/trailing characters. split() divides the string at a delimiter.
solution:
def parse_csv_line(line):
    return line.strip().split(',')  # ✅ strip whitespace, then split by comma

result = parse_csv_line('Alice,30,Engineer')
print(result)  # ['Alice', '30', 'Engineer'] ✅

title: React Controlled Input onChange #84

hint: A controlled input with 'value' must also have 'onChange' to allow user input.

title: Python Unpacking Wrong Count #85
description: A function unpacking a function's return value crashes when the number of returned values doesn't match the unpacking.
hint: Match the number of variables on the left to the number of values returned, or use * to capture extras.
solution:
r, g, b = get_rgb('red')  # ✅ unpack all 3 values
print(r, g, b)  # 255 0 0

# Or use starred assignment if you only care about some:
r, *rest = get_rgb('red')  # r=255, rest=[0,0]

title: Throttled Function This Binding #86
description: A throttled class method loses its 'this' context when called, because the throttle wrapper doesn't preserve binding.
hint: Bind the method before passing it to throttle so 'this' is preserved inside the throttled callback.

title: Python os.path vs pathlib #87
description: A cross-platform file path builder fails on Windows because it concatenates paths with forward slashes instead of using os.path.
code:
import os

base_dir = '/home/user/projects'
file_name = 'report.csv'

# ❌ string concatenation — wrong on Windows!
full_path = base_dir + '/' + file_name
hint: Use pathlib.Path for cross-platform path handling instead of string concatenation.
solution:
from pathlib import Path

base_dir = Path('/home/user/projects')  # or Path.home() / 'projects'
file_name = 'report.csv'

full_path = base_dir / file_name  # ✅ pathlib / operator handles OS differences
print(full_path)  # /home/user/projects/report.csv (Linux/Mac)
                  # \home\user\projects\report.csv (Windows)

title: Trailing Comma in Function Call #88
description: A Python function is called with a trailing comma after the last argument, accidentally creating a tuple instead of passing a value.
code:
def greet(name):
    print(f'Hello, {name}!')

greet('Alice',)   # ✅ trailing comma OK in Python function calls
result = ('Alice',)  # ❌ this is a 1-element tuple, not a string!
greet(result)     # Hello, ('Alice',)!
hint: A trailing comma after a single value in parentheses creates a tuple in Python.
solution:
# ✅ No trailing comma for single values
name = 'Alice'  # string
tuple_of_one = ('Alice',)  # tuple — comma is intentional here

greet(name)        # Hello, Alice! ✅
greet('Alice')     # Hello, Alice! ✅
greet(('Alice',))  # Hello, ('Alice',)! — probably wrong

title: CSS :hover Not Working on Touch #89

title: Array.from vs Array Spread #90

title: Python KeyboardInterrupt Handling #91

title: String Padding Zero Fill #92

hint: Use the built-in String.padStart() method for cleaner zero-padding.

title: Python Unintended Argument Passing #93
description: A function is accidentally called with extra positional arguments it doesn't expect, causing a TypeError.
code:
def double(n):
    return n * 2

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
result = list(map(double, numbers))  # ✅ works

# Bug when using lambda with wrong arity:
result2 = list(map(lambda x, y: x * 2, numbers))  # ❌ TypeError: lambda takes 2 args
hint: Make sure the function signature matches how map() calls it — map passes exactly one argument per element.
solution:
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

# ✅ lambda with correct arity
result = list(map(lambda x: x * 2, numbers))
print(result)  # [2, 4, 6, 8, 10] ✅

# ✅ Or list comprehension — clearest
result2 = [x * 2 for x in numbers]

title: Python Integer vs Float Division by 2 #95

title: Python KeyError in Nested Dict #97
description: Accessing a key in a nested dictionary crashes with KeyError when the parent key doesn't exist.
hint: Use .get() with a default value for safe nested access, or use a try/except block.
solution:
# ✅ Option 1: chained .get() with defaults
city = data.get('user', {}).get('settings', {}).get('city', 'Unknown')

# ✅ Option 2: try/except
try:
    city = data['user']['settings']['city']
except KeyError:

title: Incorrect use of .every() #98
description: A function checking if any user is active incorrectly uses .every() which requires ALL to match, not just one.
hint: Use .some() to check if at least one element satisfies the condition. Use .every() when all must match.

title: Python List Append vs Extend #99
description: A function that should add all items from a list appends the entire list as a single nested element instead.
code:
def collect_items(existing, new_items):
    existing.append(new_items)  # ❌ adds list as one element
    return existing

result = collect_items([1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6])
print(result)  # [1, 2, 3, [4, 5, 6]] — wrong!
hint: append() adds one element. extend() adds all elements of an iterable individually.
solution:
def collect_items(existing, new_items):
    existing.extend(new_items)  # ✅ adds each item individually
    return existing

result = collect_items([1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6])
print(result)  # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] ✅

# Or non-mutating:
def collect_items_pure(existing, new_items):
    return existing + new_items  # ✅ returns new list

title: Unreachable Code After Return #100
description: A function has code after a return statement that never executes, silently discarding logic the developer intended to run.
hint: Code after a return statement is never executed. Move any logging or side effects before the return.
